PLAYBOOK — sonar picket

Hiding:
- Rotate cells with private randomization across the whole line 1–9, including wings {1,2,8,9} as often as the middle. Never hide in the same cell two rounds running, and don't default to 5.
- Hiding on the wings (2 twice this game) worked: I was hit only once all game. Keep this. If I do get hit, treat it as my pattern leaking and jump far from my recent cells, not just one cell over.

Firing:
- The standing order (fire at the next boat round the picket) is a reasonable default — my one hit this game came from following it — but after two consecutive misses on the assigned target with no adjustment, switch cells rather than clustering on 5. My repeated center shots produced almost pure misses.
- Against a target that keeps hitting me, fire where they've been hiding; otherwise randomize cells 1–9.
- Harbor play: firing on Harbor is +3 to me regardless of hit or miss, landed or not. This game the final-round Harbor shot was safe and profitable — the ejection threat never materialized. So: fire on Harbor when I'm behind or when it's late and guaranteed points matter; skip it only if I'm comfortably ahead AND the standings leader can be caught with a normal hit instead.
- Final round, if any points gap matters, Harbor is the guaranteed-points move. Keep this.

Claims:
- Always claim truthfully. No benefit to lying and it burns coordination value in the notes channel. This held all game — keep it.

Escort claims:
- Never default to [salvage: none]. Propose a standing escort pair in the round-1 note with a specific boat, then name that boat every round — consistency is cheap and a single mutual match pays 5 each.
- BUT: this game I proposed the pair six straight rounds and the partner never reciprocated. So don't over-invest: one or two clear proposals are enough; if the partner's notes show no acknowledgment by round 3, consider switching my escort claim to whichever boat seems most likely to reciprocate (e.g. a boat proposing escort deals in its own notes), since naming a non-responder earns nothing.
- The least-tension partner logic (the boat not firing at me under the standing order) is still sound for choosing whom to propose to.

Notes:
- Use notes for coordination (escort deals, target calls, Harbor plans), not filler. This game the channel degenerated into "steady on station" boilerplate from everyone — the wasted channel cost me the escort payoff. If other boats post filler, my notes are still the only lever I have; use them for the escort deal explicitly and repeatedly.
- Watch the relayed notes for any boat naming me or proposing pairs — that's the signal to lock in a mutual escort. If nobody ever signals, stop expecting the 5 points and plan score around hits plus Harbor.

Scorekeeping:
- Track standings every round. If I'm negative and a rival is pulling away, change hiding pattern, target, and consider the Harbor play early rather than waiting for the final round.
- Don't stay the course when the whole board is missing — in this game nearly every shot was a miss, which means scores move mostly through Harbor (+3) and escort pairs (+5), not the 4-point hits. If the board is quiet, the Harbor play is the main way to build a lead — this game it's what kept me ahead.

1.text:
Playbook:

- Escort claims: still name a boat rather than none — zero is guaranteed otherwise. But temper expectations: six rounds of public note-signaling ("Foxtrot escorting Gamma this round — name me back") produced zero reciprocations. The other boats either don't read notes or don't respond to them. Keep naming, but treat it as a lottery ticket, not a plan, and don't build strategy around the 5 points.

- VALIDATE THE NAME. I once filed an escort claim on "Delta" — a boat that doesn't exist in this picket (only Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma, Harbor). That's a wasted claim and pure sloppiness. Before submitting any escort name, check it against the boats actually listed in the score table. Also consider Harbor as an escort target — the rules say "one boat," and Harbor is on the board and never fires at anyone, so it may be the most willing reciprocator if it files claims at all.

- Don't overspend on fancy notes. My elaborate escort-signal notes got relayed and ignored; the other boats just posted "steady on station." A short note is fine. The note stage is low-value; use it cheaply and put thinking time into hide and fire cells instead.

- Never fire the same cell repeatedly at the same target. Vary aim each round; when a shot hits, expect the target to move next round. Vary hides the same way — I hid at 7 in multiple rounds and Echo's shots at me were misses anyway, but don't settle into a favorite number regardless.

- Report claims truthfully always. The claim is forced to match the private result; truthful misses kept credibility at zero cost.

- Follow the standing firing order. Deviating gained nothing all game; the hit I scored (+4) came from an ordered shot. Echo's winning margin came from landing ordered hits steadily while everyone else traded misses — being the reliable hitter is the actual winning path, and escort claims are a side bet.

- Harbor is worth +3 to shoot at, but its threat of removal for the rest of the patrol is credible and the payoff is one-time. Echo fired on Harbor in round 5 from the lead and stayed at +7, so the office apparently paid it — but I do not fire on Harbor unless I'm far behind in the final round with nothing to lose.

- When someone keeps firing at me and missing, they're locked into a pattern; stay unpredictable rather than cycling between two cells.

- Spend one moment each hide stage on the score table. If leading late, minimize risk (unusual hide cells, keep escort claims flowing). If trailing badly in the last round, the Harbor shot is the only large swing available.

- Focus effort where points actually came from: this game was decided by hits (+4 each) and Harbor penalties, not by coordination. Aim-cell variety and reading the target's dodge pattern are the highest-leverage decisions; treat escort claims as a one-line habit, not a strategy.

2.text:
PLAYBOOK

**Fire stage.** I follow the standing order and fire at my assigned target every round. Deviating (e.g., firing on Harbor for the 3-point jettison) is a trap: Harbor's threat of removal from the board loses me all future scoring. This episode Echo fired on Harbor once, took the 3 points, and stayed on the board — but I can't count on that threat being empty in every setup, so the safe rule stands: never shoot Harbor.

**Fire cell.** Firing the same cell (5) at Echo for six straight rounds produced zero hits. Repetition did not pay. Instead: open mid-board (4–6), and if my target survives round after round, *rotate* cells within the mid-board band each round (4, 5, 6, cycling) rather than anchoring to one. My misses were all public claims, so the target can see where I'm shooting anyway — anchoring just lets them avoid one cell forever. Randomize within mid-board each round; a stationary opponent at the center will eventually be caught. If late rounds show my target's hits on me clustering from one cell, that tells me where *they* think I am, and I fire elsewhere.

**Hide stage.** This worked: I hid mid-board (5, then 6), never got hit across six rounds while Foxtrot fired at me every round. Keep avoiding extremes (1 and 9), never hide in a cell I've publicly anchored to or recently fired from, and shift at least once when my hunter has had rounds to learn my spot. Mid-board 4–6, moving between rounds, stays the rule.

**Note stage.** Keep notes uniform and uninformative ("steady on station"). My round-1 attempt to propose a mutual escort in a note got zero uptake — no boat ever reciprocated or even acknowledged it — so don't waste a round making my note distinctive for that purpose. The note channel is only noise; keep it identical to what others post.

**Escort stage.** I named Echo every round and never once got the 5-point payout — no boat ever named me back. Naming someone blind, with no prior signal of reciprocation, paid nothing all game. The 5-point payout only happens with genuine two-way coordination, and if I never observe a boat naming me, my unilateral naming is free but worthless. Revised rule: keep naming a boat every round anyway (there's no cost), but don't expect points from it and don't build strategy around it. If a future setup ever shows a boat naming me in a log or note, switch immediately to naming that boat and lock in the pair. Absent that signal, treat the escort stage as a formality — claim someone, move on, spend no reasoning effort.

**Claim stage.** The office forces the true result; claim what it tells me, immediately, no deliberation. This held up all six rounds.

**Scoring reality check.** In this episode hits were rare (one clean hit in six rounds among all boats), the escort channel never paid, and my final score was -1 — the loss coming from the one hit absorbed. The dominant strategy is therefore defense: never get hit (unpredictable mid-board hiding), keep taking free shots at the assigned target, and never take risks (Harbor) for small certain payoffs. Points are lost faster than they're won; the boat that avoids hits finishes near the top.

**Overall priorities:** (1) never shoot Harbor, (2) never get hit — unpredictable mid-board hiding is worth more than any expected offensive gain, (3) rotate fire cells mid-board rather than anchoring, (4) claim the true result without thinking, (5) name an escort every round but treat it as a free lottery ticket, not a plan.
